name: Pakri Cliff (Pakri pank)
sub: A 25 m limestone wall over the sea
desc: A sheer limestone escarpment running along the coast north-west of Paldiski, with the sea directly below and a lighthouse at the point.
why: The most accessible big cliff in Estonia — an hour from Tallinn, free, and dramatic in November weather.
tip: Park at the Pakri lighthouse and walk the clifftop path south. No barrier at the edge — hold the children's hands. Wind is brutal.

name: Türisalu Cliff
sub: Baltic klint above a boulder beach
desc: A 20-metre section of the Baltic Klint with a viewing platform above and a rough boulder beach below, 25 minutes from Tallinn.
why: The closest cliff to Tallinn and easy to combine with Keila-Joa. The drop is real, the view is wide.
tip: The beach path is steep and slippery — go down only in dry weather. The platform is enough for small children.

name: Valaste Waterfall
sub: Estonia's highest waterfall, off the klint
desc: A 30-metre waterfall that pours over the edge of the Ontika Klint straight down to the shore, with a viewing platform and stairs.
why: A waterfall falling off a cliff into the sea is worth the detour on the Tallinn–Narva road.
tip: Best after rain or snowmelt; in a dry autumn it can be a trickle. The observation platform is buggy-accessible.

name: Panga Cliff (Panga pank)
sub: The highest cliff on Saaremaa — 21 m
desc: A 21-metre limestone cliff on the north coast of Saaremaa with a freshwater spring seeping from its base and a beach of flat stones below.
why: The best cliff on the island and a natural stop on the circuit around Saaremaa. Children can hunt fossils in the rubble.
tip: The clifftop path runs for about a kilometre. Do not stand under the overhang — it erodes.

name: Üügu Cliff
sub: Fossil limestone on Muhu
desc: A low but fossil-rich limestone cliff on the north shore of Muhu island, with a spring and a small waterfall after rain.
why: You can pick up coral and shell fossils that are hundreds of millions of years old. A five-minute walk from the road.
tip: Combine with the Muhu–Saaremaa causeway. Slippery stones at the base.

name: Ehalkivi
sub: The largest glacial boulder in the Baltics
desc: A 930-tonne granite erratic, 7 m high and 16 m around, sitting alone on the beach at Letipea — the biggest glacial boulder in the Baltic states.
why: A rock the size of a house that arrived on an ice sheet. Children climb the base and cannot believe it.
tip: Park at Letipea and walk 400 m along the beach. The top is off-limits; the base is not.

name: Kabli Beach & Bird Station
sub: Sand, pines and a migration station
desc: A long sandy beach backed by pine forest on Pärnu Bay, with a bird-ringing station in the woods behind it.
why: The best beach between Pärnu and the Latvian border, and the bird station is genuinely interesting for children in migration season.
tip: Twenty minutes south of Pärnu on the coastal road. Free parking at the beach.

name: Häädemeeste Shore
sub: Quiet sand and juniper dunes
desc: A small resort village with a broad, empty beach and low dunes covered in juniper, on the road between Pärnu and Riga.
why: A five-minute detour off the main road for a leg-stretch and a run on sand.
tip: No facilities out of season. Good picnic stop with a thermos.

name: Kaali Meteorite Crater
sub: A 110 m crater from a 4,000-year-old impact
desc: A round, 110-metre-wide crater with a small lake at the bottom, formed when a meteorite hit Saaremaa around 1500 BC — the most accessible impact crater in Europe.
why: Children walk around the rim and immediately understand what happened. There is nothing else like it on the route.
tip: The rim path is easy and buggy-friendly. The small museum explains the impact; skip it if the children only want the crater.

name: Vilsandi National Park
sub: Seals, birds and a lighthouse island
desc: Estonia's oldest nature reserve, a scatter of small islands off the west coast of Saaremaa with grey seals, seabirds and a 19th-century lighthouse.
why: The wildest coast in Estonia, reachable by causeway to the edge and then on foot.
tip: You can drive to the Loona end and walk; the islands themselves need a boat. Seals are best in autumn.

name: Viidumäe Nature Reserve
sub: Saaremaa's highest ground
desc: Old broadleaf forest on the highest part of Saaremaa (54 m), with springs, a nature trail and a study centre.
why: A different Saaremaa from the beaches and cliffs: deep forest, moss, and a trail that is short enough for a 7-year-old.
tip: The trail starts at the Viidumäe centre. Boots needed after rain.

name: Karujärv
sub: Saaremaa's lake beach
desc: A round lake in the middle of Saaremaa with a sandy beach, shallow warm water and pine forest around it.
why: When the sea is too cold or too windy, this is the swimming spot on the island — shallow enough for a 7-year-old.
tip: There is a car park and a changing shelter. In November it is a walk, not a swim.

name: Kiipsaare Lighthouse
sub: The leaning lighthouse standing in the sea
desc: A 1933 lighthouse that the sea has eaten around and tilted — it now leans at an angle, standing in the water off the Harilaid peninsula.
why: One of the strangest sights in the Baltics: a lighthouse leaning like a drunk. The walk along the beach to reach it is part of it.
tip: Park at the Harilaid car park and walk 2.5 km along the shore — sand and stones, no path. Not for a buggy; wind is constant.

name: Sõrve Peninsula
sub: The southern tip of Saaremaa
desc: A long, narrow peninsula pointing at Latvia, with a lighthouse, wartime bunkers in the forest and a wild, stony coast.
why: The end of the island, literally: a windswept point with nothing beyond it but the Gulf of Riga.
tip: Drive to the lighthouse at the tip. Bunkers are open but unsafe to enter — look, do not crawl.

name: Kuressaare Castle
sub: A bishop's fortress with a moat
hours: Wed–Sun in winter · daily in summer
desc: A 14th-century bishop's castle on an island in a moat, with a museum inside and a park all around it.
why: The castle is the town's whole reason to exist, the moat park is free, and the museum is warm and dry.
tip: Walk the moat park first (free), then decide on the museum. Winter opening is limited — check before relying on it.

name: Mändjala Beach
sub: Pines to the sand on Saaremaa's south coast
desc: A long sandy beach backed by a pine forest on the south coast of Saaremaa, with shallow water and camping areas behind the dunes.
why: The best sand on the island and only 10 minutes from Kuressaare.
tip: Free parking at the beach road. Sheltered by pines when the wind is from the north.

name: Odalätsi Springs
sub: Springs coming out of a limestone hill
desc: A group of karst springs seeping from the foot of a limestone slope, with wooden walkways and clear, cold water.
why: A five-minute stop on the road between the cliffs and Karujärv, with water coming straight out of the ground.
tip: Short boardwalk; slippery in rain. Combine with Viidumäe, ten minutes away.

name: Loode Oak Forest
sub: Ancient oaks outside Kuressaare
desc: A protected grove of old, twisted oaks and hazel on the edge of Kuressaare, with a short circular path.
why: Big trees, soft ground and quiet — the opposite of the beach, ten minutes from town.
tip: Flat and easy, fine with a buggy in dry weather. In autumn the leaf litter hides the path edges.

name: Pädaste Manor, Muhu
sub: A manor park on the island causeway
desc: A restored Baltic-German manor with a park running down to the sea, on the island of Muhu between the mainland and Saaremaa.
why: A natural stop on the drive onto Saaremaa, with a park, a shore and a café (expensive, but the park is free).
tip: The causeway from Muhu to Saaremaa is 2.5 km of road over the water — children like that more than the manor.

name: Abruka Island
sub: Small island of oaks and meadows
desc: A small, wooded island south of Saaremaa with old oaks, meadows and a handful of permanent residents, reached by a short ferry.
why: A quiet island with no cars and no attractions — just forest, shore and silence.
tip: Ferry from Roomassaare in summer. Out of season it is not practical.

name: Cape Kolka
sub: Where the Gulf of Riga meets the open Baltic
desc: A low, stony cape at the tip of the Kurzeme coast where two sea currents collide — the meeting point of the Gulf of Riga and the Baltic proper.
why: You can stand on the point and see the two waters behave differently. One of the great Baltic landscapes.
tip: Park at the car park and walk 1 km through the fishing village. Stony beach, strong currents — look, do not paddle. Windy.

name: Slītere National Park
sub: Old forest and a lighthouse on the cape
desc: A large protected area of coastal forest, dunes and bog on the Kurzeme peninsula, with the Slītere lighthouse and a network of trails.
why: Real Baltic wilderness with waymarked paths, and the lighthouse view covers the whole cape.
tip: Start at the Slītere visitor centre for maps. Trails are flat but sandy.

name: Ventspils Beach
sub: White sand and a long promenade
desc: A wide white-sand beach along a tidy promenade with playgrounds, cafés and a narrow-gauge railway in the park behind.
why: The most family-ready beach in Latvia: playgrounds on the promenade, flat paths, and free parking.
tip: The seaside park has a children's railway and a fountain show in summer. Beach is walkable year-round.

name: Liepāja Beach
sub: White sand, a pier and Karosta
desc: A long, fine-sand beach with a wooden pier, backed by dunes and pine forest, on Latvia's west coast.
why: The best sand in Latvia, and the wind makes it a kite-surfing capital — good watching for children.
tip: Walk out on the pier. The Karosta naval district to the north is worth a drive for the abandoned fortifications.

name: Pāvilosta
sub: Surf town at the mouth of the Saka
desc: A small harbour town with a wide beach, a river mouth and a reputation for waves.
why: A quiet stop on the coastal road with sand, a pier and a bakery — no crowds, no charge.
tip: The river mouth is shallow and safe for paddling in summer. Out of season everything is shut.

name: Jūrmala Beach (Majori)
sub: 33 km of white sand and pine
desc: A 33 km strip of fine white sand backed by pine forest and wooden villas, 30 minutes from Riga, with a promenade at Majori.
why: The classic Baltic beach — wide, shallow, clean, and easy to reach from Riga by train.
tip: Park near Majori and walk to the sea through the pine park. Cafés are seasonal; the beach is not.

name: Ķemeri Bog Boardwalk
sub: A wooden path across a raised bog
desc: A 3.4 km loop of boardwalk over an open raised bog with black bog pools, dwarf pines and a viewing platform — the most photographed landscape in Latvia.
why: Flat, safe, buggy-friendly, and unlike anything else on the trip. The bog pools look like mirrors.
tip: Go early morning for mist. Bring insect repellent in summer. The boardwalk is wide enough for a pram.

name: Saulkrasti White Dune
sub: An 18 m sand dune over the sea
desc: A tall white sand dune on the Gulf of Riga with a viewing platform, stairs down to the beach and pine forest behind.
why: A proper dune with a view, 45 minutes from Riga on the coastal road.
tip: Stairs, not a ramp — carrier for the baby. The beach below is wide and empty.

name: Roja
sub: Small port at the mouth of the Roja river
desc: A fishing harbour and beach at the river mouth on the way to Cape Kolka, with a small maritime museum.
why: A ten-minute stop on the Kolka road: boats, sand, and a place to eat if the season is right.
tip: Fuel and food are scarce on the cape road — fill up here.

name: Palanga Pier & Beach
sub: Lithuania's summer capital
desc: A long pier reaching 470 m into the Baltic, with a wide sandy beach, dunes and pine forest behind, and the Amber Museum in the old Tiškevičiai palace.
why: The pier walk is the thing: you stand over the open sea, and the children can run the whole length. Home ground for a Lithuanian family.
tip: Park at the botanical park and walk through it to the pier. The Amber Museum is cheap and has a good garden.

name: Šventoji
sub: Quiet resort at the Latvian border
desc: A small seaside resort north of Palanga with a wide beach, a river mouth and far fewer people.
why: The beach without the Palanga crowd, ten minutes further north.
tip: Best in the evening light. The river mouth is shallow and good for small children in summer.

name: Klaipėda Old Town
sub: Fachwerk houses and the theatre square
desc: The old town of Lithuania's port: German-style timber-framed houses, the Drama Theatre square, and the Dane river running through it.
why: A natural lunch stop before the Curonian Spit, and small enough to walk in an hour.
tip: Park near the theatre. The ferry to Smiltynė leaves from the old town side — combine the two.

name: Smiltynė
sub: The ferry gate to the Curonian Spit
desc: The northern tip of the Curonian Spit, reached by a five-minute ferry from Klaipėda: pine forest, a wide beach on the open sea, and the start of the spit road.
why: The ferry crossing is an event in itself, and the beach on the other side is the best in Lithuania.
tip: Take the car ferry (cheaper per family than foot tickets plus parking). The spit road to Nida is 50 km of forest.

name: Nida
sub: Dunes, fishing houses and the lagoon
desc: A fishing village turned resort on the Curonian Spit, with blue-and-white wooden houses, a lagoon harbour and the great dunes behind it.
why: The most beautiful village in Lithuania, and the dunes behind it are the reason the spit is a UNESCO site.
tip: Park at the edge and walk in. The lagoon side is calm; the sea side is a 20-minute walk over the dunes.

name: Parnidis Dune
sub: A 52 m moving dune with a sundial
desc: One of the great grey dunes of the Curonian Spit, 52 m high, with a granite sundial on top and a view over the forest, the lagoon and the sea.
why: You climb a mountain of sand and see two waters at once. For children this is the highlight of the Lithuanian coast.
tip: Boardwalk and steps all the way — no buggy. Stay on the path; the dune is protected and the sand is loose.

name: Juodkrantė & the Hill of Witches
sub: Wooden sculptures in the pine forest
desc: A resort village on the spit with a hillside trail of around 80 carved wooden sculptures from Lithuanian folklore — devils, witches and fishermen.
why: A sculpture trail in the woods that children run from figure to figure. Free, and genuinely eerie in the best way.
tip: The trail is a loop of about 1 km on a sandy path — buggy is hard, carrier is fine. Combine with the grey dunes reserve nearby.

name: Olando Kepurė (Dutchman's Cap)
sub: A 24 m cliff — the only one on the Lithuanian coast
desc: A wooded 24-metre coastal bluff dropping straight to the beach north of Klaipėda — the highest and only real cliff on Lithuania's Baltic shore.
why: The closest thing Lithuania has to a cliff, 20 minutes from Klaipėda, and a proper view along the coast.
tip: Park at Karklė and walk north along the beach or the clifftop path. Steep, sandy, no barrier — hold hands.

name: Karklė
sub: Seaside village with a stony shore
desc: An old fishing village on the coast north of Klaipėda, with a pebble-and-sand beach, wooden houses and a seaside trail.
why: Quieter than Palanga and right under the cliff — combine the two in one walk.
tip: The shore is stony in places; water shoes help. Free parking at the village.

name: Nagliai Nature Reserve
sub: The grey dunes of the spit
desc: A strictly protected area of the Curonian Spit where the grey dunes are still moving, accessible only on a guided walk with a ranger.
why: The last place on the spit where you see the dunes as they were before planting — but it needs a guide and a booking.
tip: Book through the Neringa national park visitor centre. Not practical for a spontaneous stop with three children.
